entries.a: Escrow is a neutral third party that holds money and documents until every condition of the purchase agreement has been met. The buyer deposits earnest money, the seller takes the property off the market, and neither the funds nor the property move again until the terms are satisfied. That's the whole idea: nobody has to trust the other side, because we hold it.

A standard Southern California residential resale runs 30 to 45 days, driven almost entirely by the lender. All-cash can close in 10 to 14 days. What actually causes delays: late loan approval, title issues found on the preliminary report, unsigned documents, and HOA document turnaround.

In Southern California the escrow fee is customarily split 50/50 between buyer and seller. The seller customarily pays the owner's title policy and the county transfer tax; the buyer customarily pays the lender's title policy and their loan costs. All of it is negotiable in the purchase agreement — the contract always wins over custom.

Escrow fees scale with the sale price. Rather than quote you a number I might get wrong, run it through our net sheet tool — it uses our published fee schedule and shows every line item. If anything looks off, an officer will walk you through it.

A net sheet estimates what a seller actually walks away with after commissions, payoffs, taxes and fees — or what a buyer needs to bring to closing. You can run one yourself on our net sheet page in about two minutes, and put your own name and brokerage on the PDF.

Earnest money is the buyer's good-faith deposit, usually 1–3% of the purchase price, wired to escrow shortly after the contract is signed. It's not an extra cost — it's credited toward the down payment at closing. Whether it's refundable depends on which contingencies are still in place.

entries.q: How do I send my wire safely?
entries.a: Three rules, and they matter more than anything else in the transaction. One: never take wiring instructions from an email, even one that looks like ours. Two: call your escrow officer at the number you already have — not a number in the email — and verify the instructions verbally. Three: Wonderland never changes wire instructions mid-transaction. If you get an email saying we did, it's fraud. Call us.

entries.q: What is a preliminary title report?
entries.a: The preliminary title report shows what's recorded against the property: liens, easements, judgments, unpaid taxes, and anything else that has to be cleared before ownership can transfer cleanly. We read every one carefully, because title problems are one of the most common reasons a closing slips.

Contingencies are the buyer's exit ramps, each tied to a condition being met: the inspection, the appraisal coming in at or above price, financing being approved, clear title, and sometimes the sale of the buyer's current home. While a contingency is active the buyer can renegotiate or withdraw. Once it's removed, the deposit is generally at risk.

entries.q: What do I need to bring to signing?
entries.a: A valid government-issued photo ID that isn't expired — that's the one people get caught out by. Everything else we send ahead of time. Signings happen at our office, by mobile notary, or remotely depending on your lender's requirements.

entries.q: When do I get my money as a seller?
entries.a: Once the deed records, your proceeds go out the same day by wire, or by check if you prefer. Wires sent before the bank's cutoff typically post the same day; after cutoff they queue and land the next business day. Your officer will email you the moment it's sent.

entries.q: Can you help with a 1031 exchange?
entries.a: Yes — several of our officers handle 1031 exchanges regularly, along with refinances, mobile homes, lease land, and commercial transactions. Because exchanges are deadline-driven and unforgiving, tell us early so we can coordinate with your qualified intermediary from day one.

Five offices across Southern California: Sherman Oaks (818) 650-8950, Santa Clarita (661) 210-3615, Westlake Village (805) 869-1790, Rancho Mirage (760) 248-3070, and La Quinta (760) 895-6380. Every officer's direct line and email is on their office page.

Send us the fully executed purchase agreement and the contact details for both agents, and we'll open the file and issue escrow instructions the same business day. You can start that on our Open Escrow page, or call the office nearest the property.

entries.q: What information do you need to open escrow?
entries.a: From the seller's side: the complete street address and parcel number if you have it, full legal names and marital status of all sellers with addresses and phone numbers, whether the property is owner-occupied or a rental, every lender and lien holder to be paid off (company, loan number, address, phone, approximate balance), the HOA name and management company contact, and any reports already in hand — termite, home protection, natural hazard. From the buyer's side: full names and marital status of all buyers, how they want to take title, new lender information, and fire or hazard insurance details. If a married couple is involved, we need both spouses' full legal names, not just one.

entries.q: What is a Statement of Information?
keywords: why do you need my ssn
entries.a: It's a confidential form the title company uses to tell you apart from other people with similar names — so someone else's judgment or lien doesn't attach to your file. Sellers are required to provide it to the escrow holder within seven days of contract acceptance. It goes to the title officer to help clear title, not into any public record.

entries.q: What documents end up in my escrow file?
entries.a: By the time we close, the file holds the purchase contract with all counters and addendums, the deposit receipt, escrow instructions and every amendment, the preliminary title report, the natural hazard disclosure, geological and flood disclosures, payoff statements for any liens, hazard insurance, the home warranty policy, HOA documents if applicable, city reports and retrofit certification where required, a copy of any trust or corporate documents, the foreign-status affidavit if it applies, and the closing statement.

It's normally agreed between buyer and seller, and if an agent is involved they'll often recommend one. It is genuinely your choice, though — you can ask for a specific escrow holder in the purchase agreement, and it's worth checking who you're actually handing your funds to before you do.

entries.q: What is the difference between an independent and a controlled escrow company?
entries.a: An independent escrow company is licensed and examined by the state and must meet bonding, trust-account and financial requirements. A controlled escrow operates under an exemption — typically inside a broker, title company, bank or attorney's practice. Both are legal; they're regulated differently. If you want to know which you're dealing with, ask directly and ask who audits their trust account.

Prorations divide ongoing costs between buyer and seller at the closing date, so each pays only for the days they owned the property. Property taxes, HOA dues, and sometimes rent and security deposits on tenant-occupied property all get prorated. They show as debits and credits on the closing statement.

The closing statement is the full accounting of your transaction: every credit, every debit, every fee, and the bottom-line figure you receive or bring. Ask for an estimated one up front rather than at the signing table — that's the moment to question anything you don't recognize, not after funds have moved.

entries.q: What do funding and recording mean?
entries.a: Funding is when the lender releases the loan proceeds to escrow. Recording is when the county recorder enters the deed in the public record and ownership legally transfers. Escrow closes on recording — that's the moment the property is yours, and it's why a same-day funding delay can push a closing to the next business day.

entries.q: What happens if escrow is cancelled?
entries.a: We can only release funds on written instructions signed by both parties, or on a court order — a cancellation isn't something one side can do unilaterally through us. Third-party costs already incurred, like the title search or reports, are generally still owed. Whether the deposit is refundable comes down to which contingencies were still in place, which is a contract question for your agent.

Yes. A refinance runs through escrow much like a purchase, minus the transfer of ownership: we take the new lender's instructions, order the payoff on your existing loan, coordinate signing, and record the new deed of trust. Shop a few lenders before you commit — the terms vary more than most people expect.
